newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-AWB pleased with Iran wheat price.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-AWB pleased with Iran wheat price.

text.p: Australia's 1.5 million tonne wheat sale to Iran was priced at about the same level as the recent sale to Pakistan, Trevor Flugge, chairman of the Australian Wheat Board (AWB), told Reuters on Friday.
Flugge would not disclose price in the Australian Standard White (ASW) sale to Iran, but said it more than supported the current ASW pool level of A$185 a tonne.
As previously reported, Australia's sale of 112,000 tonnes of ASW to Pakistan this week was priced at US$156.285 a tonne fob.
"It's a very good price (for the sale to Iran) and we're very very comfortable with it," Flugge said. "It would have been probably in the same ballpark (as the sale to Pakistan)."
"Pricing today is such that we're very comfortable with it, we're finding that it's not a problem," he said.

While the sale to Iran made that country Australia's biggest wheat customer, sales to Egypt were also going extremely well on a monthly basis, while the AWB's normal markets into Asia were also good, he said.
The Indonesian market had been very good so far for new crop wheat and it was expected that there would be more significant sales there in the next month, Flugge said.
"Basically our bulk markets have gone very well," he said.
New markets also in Sudan, India, Turkey, Nigeria, southern and eastern Africa and South America, while not for big tonnages, were "ticking along niclely," he said.
But the bulk markets had come in very strongly, he said.

World markets were tough for a while in November, especially with Argentina discounting on price. But recognition had emerged that while Argentina had a big crop it also had logistical problems which were not easily overcome, Flugge said.

Argentina's available export tonnages were not that significant in relation to six-month world usages, and demand was still increasing, with most countries purchasing more wheat than last year, he said.
With prices high last year, most markets then bought "hand-to-mouth". Significantly lower prices this year were producing some re-building of strategic stocks.
An aggressive marketing strategy by the AWB, Australia's monopoly wheat exporter, mainly involved putting people on the ground in significant markets and did not involve price-cutting, Flugge said.
"Even though we had a big crop we were not going to be forced into a ridiculous situation where we just tried to outbid one other," he said.
That was recognised by most major sellers, including Canada, Europe and the U.S., he said.
The AWB's strategy had been to hold off from entering into price warfare with Argentina in the belief that the discounting problem would dissipate, he said.
It had not dissipated fully yet, but Australia was not prepared to chase the price down, he said.
With some of its best quality wheat in 1997 for many years, Australia had the opportunity to supply what markets wanted.
AWB would make further "significant sales" in the coming month, Flugge predicted, although he would not reveal specifics.
The organisation first would wait for the market to react to the Iran sale, he said.
Australia's current 1996/97 wheat crop is estimated at about 21.5 million tonnes but some trade sources believed it could go higher to top the 22 million tonne record set in 1983/84.
Other information from the AWB is that several big cash tenders remain in the world market.

Pakistan is seen as requiring 500,000 tonnes, Bangladesh 100,000 tonnes optional origin wheat for delivery before February 21 and Egypt 500,000 tonnes, while Iraq is in the market for an undisclosed tonnage of French wheat.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
